_what: What players read after an update, and the rule the version number follows. Written for players: plain words, no ticket numbers (a ticket number never reaches a player). `scripts/bump_version.mjs` moves `next` into `releases` under the version it cuts, and decides that version by the rule below.

rule.patch: The last number moves with every update.
rule.minor: The middle number moves on the update that brings the fifth new feature since the last time it moved.
rule.major: The first number moves only when the game becomes a different game for someone already playing — a save that cannot carry forward, a change to how every roll, fight or advance works, or a new era of the world — and only by Erik's call.

kinds.feature: something a player can now do or see that they could not before
kinds.fix: something that behaved wrong and now behaves right
kinds.change: a rule or a number that moved
kinds.internal: work a player never meets — recorded, never shown

entries.title: A cart that travels alone, and what that costs
entries.summary: Sending a load with nobody walking beside it now loses more than losing a fight does — and the card says so before you set the route.
entries.detail: What a robbery on the road takes was the same number as what a raid on a hold takes, because the road was reading the hold's dial. Nobody had decided it for a road. The road has its own two numbers now: losing a fight still costs half the load, and a cart nobody walks with costs three quarters — more than losing, because bringing people should never be the worse choice. Losing everything is still reserved for a load whose whole escort was killed. The trade card also stopped assuming two carriers for every holding: it forecasts the hands the hold actually has, which for most holdings is none. So a card that used to quote wages for people who do not exist now says plainly that the cart will go out alone, and what the road will take for it — which is usually a better reason to hire carriers than their speed.

entries.title: Carriers you can hire, so your own people stay home
entries.summary: Four trade companies will carry a hold's whole output to market for a share of what it sells for — their animals, their guards, their roads.
entries.detail: The hold's card now lists them beside selling at home and sending your own cart, in the same unit as everything else: what it earns in a pass. The Hub Yard Porters take 22% and walk anywhere the gate network reaches; the Hundred-Market Carters are cheaper at 18% but answer to the Undercount and only work four regions; the Keelmouth Slip Lighters go by water and do not trust the gates; the Asking Floor Factors are the most expensive in the world and have never lost a load. Hiring them is a standing arrangement — every pass their people come, take what the hold has made, and bring back your share. Whether it beats your own carriers depends on the road: on a long haul through a gate they know and you do not, the Porters turn a 135-day walk into two days; on a short safe road their cut is simply money you kept before. Their guards walk with the load and fight for it, and a bad enough road still beats them.

entries.title: A cart now travels at the speed the card quoted
entries.summary: The comparison table priced a stable, a river or a hired company's animals into the journey, and then every cart went on foot.
entries.detail: The speed table — on foot, a stable, a lizard-den, by water, a hired company — was read only where routes are priced, never where a cart is actually sent. Nobody noticed because no hold in the world owns a stable, so the quoted journey and the walked one agreed by coincidence; hiring a company with its own animals is the first thing that made them differ, and it differed by half. Journeys now take the days the card promised, which also means fewer days on a dangerous road — a faster route really is a safer one now, not just a cheaper-looking one. Two other places where the quote and the journey disagreed are fixed with it: a company that knows the gates now walks the gates when it carries for you, and the news that says a load has left no longer reports nobody walking beside it when six hired guards are.

entries.title: A market charges for the right to sell, and standing decides what
entries.summary: Eleven markets are held by a power now, and each asks a flat fee per load — waived if they trust you, doubled if they do not, shut if they hate you.
entries.detail: Millbrook asks two shards to the Council's box by the well; the Grand Lattice deducts eight at Intake before you knew you had agreed. The hold's card shows whose market it is, what they ask, and subtracts it from every way of moving the store — selling here, the keeper's pass, and a standing run — so the number you compare against is the number you pay. Get on good terms and it is waived; fall out of them and it doubles; fall all the way and they will not let you sell there at all, and the load goes home or on to the next market. A place no power holds still charges nothing, which is most of the world.

entries.title: Some wardens are corrupt, and the price depends on who is asking
entries.summary: At two of the eleven markets the fee is what the wardens say it is today.
entries.detail: The Undercount and the Barony at Firstsight have corrupt wardens — a trait of the wardens, not of the lord, because a fair lord can have crooked men. Their fee rises for a stranger and for anyone plainly carrying, and falls for somebody they know. If the power itself has shut its market to you, theirs can still be opened by coin into the right hand. And the coin never reaches the power: pay a corrupt market and their lord is no better disposed to you for it — but stand in their market and say publicly what they are taking, and the power itself will think better of you. The wardens will not forget it.

entries.title: The game asks before it invents somebody you have already met
entries.summary: A stranger whose office matches someone you know is a question now, not a second record.
entries.detail: Before anyone new is written down, the GM is shown the people you already know who could plausibly be here — seen in the last few days, last known to be here or one road away, or answering to somebody this scene already names — with the instruction that a person you have met is never introduced as a stranger. And when a stranger turns up in the same office as someone you know (the same post, the same master, word for word), they are NOT written down until the GM says whether it is the same person or a different one. It says which, once, and if they are different you will never be asked about that pair again.

entries.title: Saying "that is the same person" now moves everything
entries.summary: Merging two records left your party, your quests and your codex pointing at the record that was deleted.
entries.detail: The merge on a person's card folded their notes together and then left every other reference behind — the party entry, a quest they gave you, a hold they keep, what your codex knows. It moves all of it now, and tells you how many records moved; the times you have spoken to them add up instead of being overwritten; and the id that was folded away is remembered, so anything written against the old one still finds them. The list of people to merge with puts the likely matches at the top, with the reason.

entries.title: One person, one record
entries.summary: People you met twice — once as a stranger and once by name — were two different people in your records. They are one now.
entries.detail: When you meet someone before you learn their name, the game writes down the stranger; when they give their name, it was writing down a second person. Your save is repaired on the next load, and the game tells you which one was which: "You realise the Radiant authority sent to intercept was Vail Langley." Everything that pointed at the stranger — your party, a quest they gave you, a hold they keep, what your codex knows, what is still owed — now points at the person, and the bond you earned, the times you have spoken and the day you first met are all kept. If two people in your records could BOTH be the stranger, nothing is merged: guessing between two people is worse than waiting for you to say.

entries.title: Anyone who will come can walk with you
entries.summary: Asking someone to join your party said they refused. They were not refusing — and often they had already joined.
entries.detail: Two things were wrong at once. The number of people you can bring FORWARD is what closeness earns, and that limit was also turning away anyone who simply wanted to travel with you — so a full party meant every new ask came back as "They will not come." And underneath it, the picker was reporting a refusal even when the person had joined, then throwing the join away. Both are fixed: anyone who will come walks with you, the ones closeness has earned a named place come forward, and the rest stand in the line and are told so. A real refusal now says what it is instead of blaming the person.

entries.title: "Keep out of it" keeps them out of it
entries.summary: Telling someone to hang back did nothing at all — the order was recorded and never read.
entries.detail: The button wrote the order down and nothing in the game ever looked at it, so the label never changed and the person stayed in the line and in every fight. Now one reader answers for the whole game: the card says "Back into the line", nothing targets them, and they are out of it until you say otherwise.

entries.title: Your people are named, and what they bring is read
entries.summary: On some screens the people travelling with you showed as raw ids, with no skills behind them.
entries.detail: Almost everyone you meet in play lives only in your own record of them, and two screens were only looking in the authored catalogue — so those people arrived with no name and nothing on their sheet: a champion with no crafts, a mender counted as one more sword. They are read from both now, wherever their record lives, and what each of them brings is the whole of it rather than whichever half the screen happened to ask for.

entries.title: A recap that fails says so
entries.summary: When a session recap could not be written, nothing appeared and nothing explained why.
entries.detail: The apology had been written and saved for months and was never shown on screen. It shows now, and the button offers to try again.

entries.title: A waygate stands outside the town now, not in it
entries.summary: Fifteen cities kept their gate in the middle of the streets. The gate is an hour and a half out, in a yard, and the walk in is yours to make.
entries.detail: Step through toward Bedrock and you arrive at the Weighed Arch: a walled yard of numbered flagstones with a weigh-house on the town side and a clerk who writes down what came through. The Crossing has the Hub Yard, where the world arrives and is walked in by porters who know the city. Aiming at a town still works — the gate takes you to its yard, and the town is ninety minutes down the road. The reason is what it means for anyone ELSE coming through: a raiding party cannot appear in a market square any more. It lands in the yard, outside the walls, with open ground to cross, and whoever stands watch has a far better chance of seeing it come.

entries.title: The gates you had already found are still yours
entries.summary: A gate you discovered at a town is the same gate now that it stands outside it.
entries.detail: Your record of where you have been named the town, and the gate moved out of the town — so without this every gate you had found at one of the fifteen would have become a gate you had never heard of. They are all still there, under the yard's name, and the world tells you so once.

entries.title: Maintenance
A waygate costs you nothing but the hours
entries.summary: Stepping through a gate no longer takes energy — only the time it takes.
entries.detail: A gate leg used to cost ten energy on top of the hours through the arch. It costs nothing now, for you, for a load on a trade route and for a hired company alike: a gate is still not a free teleport, because it takes real hours and you have to have found it first, but it will never again leave you short of the strength to do what you went there for.

entries.title: The great figures push the arcs they were written to push
entries.summary: Thirteen figures carried their stake in a world arc on a record the game never read.

entries.title: The worst ground in the world has its name
entries.summary: Danger 5 reads “forsaken” on the map and in a place's own line.
entries.detail: When the danger scale gained its top rung it needed a word, and it had a placeholder — “unsurvivable” — while the right one was being chosen. It is “forsaken”: the sixteen places that carry it are ground the world has given up on, and the only ground a legendary creature walks.

entries.title: A great figure can finish what they started
entries.summary: An arc that runs to its end without anyone stopping it now has a consequence, and the world says so.
entries.detail: The great figures of the world have been leaning on its long arcs for a while — some driving one forward, others holding it back — and an arc could reach its end with nothing happening. Now the figure who drove it there has done the thing their arc was about, and the world changes to suit it. If someone is standing in their way, they arrive anyway and the two of them are locked against each other, which is exactly when your help matters most. ⚠️ And if you go and stop that figure first — or whoever was standing in their way falls to somebody else — what happens next is different. The news tells you a figure has finished; what they finished into is the GM's to reveal.

entries.title: Your holdings, at a glance
entries.summary: The Holdings screen opens with four readings — how many places, what they do to your purse each pass, who stands at them, and how many want you — and a list of exactly what wants you, each with the button that answers it.
entries.detail: The screen used to open with a thin line and a wall of cards. It now opens the way the design for it always intended: four boards across the top, the last one outlined when something needs a decision from you; then “To review” — one row per place that wants something, saying what it wants and carrying the button that goes straight to the tab where you do it. Underneath, the places themselves are two to a row, each with its condition beside its name, its keeper, how many people stand there, and what it pays you a pass, under labels so you can read down the column instead of hunting. On a phone they stack to one column. ⚠️ And the three surfaces now count the same things: the board, the list and the cards ask one reader, so a place cannot be quietly urgent on its card and missing from the list.

entries.title: Your party reads like the rest of it
entries.summary: Who walks with you, what they bring, how often it lands and where they stand — under labels, with the state of the line said in plain lines instead of one grey sentence.
entries.detail: The party screen carries the same shapes as the holdings one: chips across the top for how the party stands, then “how the line stands” — one line per condition, amber when something is holding you back — and a card each, with what they bring, how often their craft lands, and whether they are brought forward or in the line. Everything you could do before you can still do: stance, bringing someone forward, starring the crafts you would rather they used.

entries.title: Your purse reads as money
entries.summary: Scrip was printed with sixteen decimal places and named by its internal id.
entries.detail: A purse holding another Reach's scrip read “899.9700000000001 the_palelands scrip” — the number a rate produced rather than the money you have, and the region's key instead of its name. It says “899.97 The Palelands scrip” now, wherever the purse is shown.

entries.title: Tell a hold what to do with its stock
entries.summary: Keep all of it, keep up to a number and sell the rest, or sell what the keeper can each pass — for the whole store or one good at a time.
entries.detail: A hold's keeper sells a share of the store every pass at the local price. Now you decide how much of it she is allowed to sell: keep everything, keep up to a number of units and sell the rest, or let her sell what she can. The line beside the control says what she will actually sell this pass, and the raid warning underneath says what the stock she is standing on costs you — which is the whole decision: goods are worth more on a caravan than in a shed, and worth nothing at all to a hold that is raided. A run standing out of the hold sets the policy by itself: nobody sells what the caravan is waiting for.

entries.title: Three characters get their people's crafts back
entries.summary: A character whose record named their people by an old name was being handed none of the basics that people is born to.
entries.detail: Peoples were renamed a while ago — "valley" became Valleyfolk, "radiant" the Radiant Plateau — and three saves still carried the old name. Because nothing in the game could find a people by a name that no longer existed, those characters were given none of the crafts their people are born to, no home region, and no innate reach into the substrate. Their records are corrected on the next load, the withheld basics are handed over, and the game says which ones they are.

entries.title: A recovered save keeps the quests it finished
entries.summary: Merging a recovered copy could drop every quest ending it held.
entries.detail: A chronicle holds two kinds of entry: a line about a scene, and the full record of a quest's ending — its outcome, what was said, the day. When a recovered copy was merged into a live one, the check for "do I already have this" could not tell one ending from another, so a save that already held one quest ending would refuse every ending the recovered copy brought. Fixed, and the merge now counts them properly.

entries.title: The raid-risk line now says what your watch is worth
entries.summary: Beside what a raid would cost you a pass, the readout now shows what it costs if your watch beats the raids it sees coming.
entries.detail: The line under a hold's store used to say a raid came "about 1 in 25 passes" and what standing on the stock cost you — and the cost never once asked whether anybody was watching, although the sentence implied it did. Now it does: the same contest that decides whether a raid is seen is read straight into the number, so a hold with people on watch shows both ends — what the stock costs you if every raid takes its share, and what it costs if the ones your watch sees are beaten off. A full store on bad ground with nobody watching runs about 13 a pass; two on watch halves the chance and, if they win the fights they start, brings it under 4.

entries.title: A hold can run a standing trade route
entries.summary: Set a run from a hold's card and it keeps running — every departure carries what the place has made since the last one.
entries.detail: Until now a load only left a hold when the story sent one. Now the comparison on a hold's card has a button beside every market: set the run, and the hold's carriers walk it again and again on their own. While a run stands, whoever keeps the place holds the stock back for the cart instead of selling it locally, so each departure carries everything made since the last one — and the carriers walk home afterwards, which is why a far market gets a cart less often than a near one. Stop the run and the keeper starts selling here again.

entries.title: Distance is a wait and a risk, not a discount
entries.summary: A far market no longer divides what you earn by the days on the road. It delays the first coin, and it puts your stock in danger while it waits.
entries.detail: Trade used to be priced as though a caravan were a single trip: the take divided by the days, which meant a market three times richer and fifty days away could never be worth walking to. A route is not a trip — it runs again and again, and in the long run everything the place makes reaches the market. So each way of moving the store now shows what it earns in a pass, with two honest costs beside it: when the first coin comes back, and what the stock waiting for the cart risks while it stands in the shed. A hold you cannot defend is the reason a long run loses — not the distance itself.

entries.title: Stables, lizard-dens and rivers move a load faster
entries.summary: A hold's own animals carry a load in half the time; a lizard-den better still; and water, if both ends are on it, faster than either.
entries.detail: A stable or a boat-house on the hold puts a load on the road at twice the speed, a lizard-den at two and a half, and a river or harbour at both ends at three — you take the fastest way you have, never all of them at once. Because trouble on the road is rolled for each day travelled, a faster road is a safer one as well. This is what a stable is FOR on a trading hold.

entries.title: A road you have walked gets safer
entries.summary: Each completed run cuts the trouble on that road by a tenth, down to half — and a relay station of yours on the way doubles how fast it learns.
entries.detail: The people who walk a road learn it: the fords, the hours, who to avoid. Every load that arrives cuts that road's danger by a tenth, to a floor of half, and a road is known in both directions. A relay station of yours standing on the route doubles the rate. It counts on arrival, not on setting out — a load that was taken on the way taught nobody anything.

entries.title: Loads take the fastest way, including your waygates
entries.summary: A cart was walking the long road to places your own gate reaches in an afternoon.
entries.detail: When a load left a hold it took the first way the map offered, which was always the road — so a run the card priced at under two days could walk thirty-four. It now takes the fastest way its carriers can actually use, gates included.

entries.title: Somebody is standing in the way, and does not know what of
entries.summary: Two of the world's seven worst positions are held — not by something terrible, but by a woman who simply will not move. A villain who gets past her takes the position; while she stands, none of them can.
entries.detail:
One has buried more than she has known and never stopped attending, so she refuses neither the dying nor the living. The other unmakes only what should end, and then stops. Neither of them is stronger than the things reaching past her — that is the point: restraint is thinner, and it holds anyway.

So the most consequential thing you can do on either of those two fronts is keep her alive. Kill her, turn her, or break her and the position opens — to whoever did it, and to nobody else. A rockfall does not hand anybody a throne.

⛑ And neither woman knows she is holding a seat. She knows what she is holding back. Ask her why she stays and she will tell you about the dying, or about what should end — not about the shape of the world.

entries.title: And one of the seven has nobody in the way of it at all
entries.summary: The Chaos / Order seat is open, one figure is walking toward it, and nothing stands between.
entries.detail: The other six either have somebody in them or somebody blocking them. This one has neither. It needs no war and no removal — only for that figure to finish what they are doing, which the lore calls the most dangerous position in the world for exactly that reason.

entries.title: Everyone has a name underneath what they are called
entries.summary: A hundred and twelve of the world's great figures now have a whole name — given, middle, family — and most of them nobody says out loud.
entries.detail:
The Unbound is what everyone calls them. Underneath it they are somebody, and for a third of the world's figures that name is hidden: the game knows it, and you do not. Another third is known only to scholars, kin and the old. The rest is common knowledge, and those you will see on the card as soon as you meet them.

What people call them never changes — that is the name in the world's mouth, and epithets sit beside it rather than inside it. ⛑ And a hidden name is never quietly matchable: the game will not answer to a name nobody told you.

entries.title: A name is something you can learn
entries.summary: Hidden names are reachable — by a craft that asks beyond the Veil, by somebody who trades in them, or by the fiction handing one over.
entries.detail: Learn one and it is yours: the card shows it from then on, for your character and nobody else's. This is why it matters that it was hidden — there are crafts in this world that work on a true name, and a name you had to earn is worth something a name printed on a card is not.

entries.title: A hidden name was one commit from being in a tooltip
entries.summary: The people card put the whole name in its hover without asking whether you were allowed to see it.
entries.detail: It had been written that way long before there were any hidden names to leak, and it read straight off the record. The moment a hundred and twelve whole names landed, a third of them hidden, the hover would have quietly handed them over. It asks first now — and it asks the world's own record rather than your character's copy, because a thin copy with no answer would have been read as “everybody knows this one”.

entries.title: Eleven things that work, and cost
entries.summary: A ring nothing can be hidden from. A coin that gets you a yes every time. A seal that keeps a living body exactly as it was. Each does what it says — and each takes something you did not agree to.
entries.detail:
They are not upgrades. The ring means nothing near you can be concealed, and it means you cannot hide either — not a penalty, an impossibility: while you are wearing it there is no sneaking, no disguise, no secret kept, and the game will tell you so in the ring's own words rather than letting you roll and fail. The lantern shows every hidden thing and cannot be dimmed, so everything sees you too. The narrator is told exactly what each one does and what it costs, and told the cost is not optional.

And every one of them is a thing somebody already learned to recognise: holding one counts as having seen its mark.

entries.title: Using one helps somebody you have not met
entries.summary: Every use of one of these feeds the thing that wants what it is for — and you are not told.
entries.detail: That is the point of them. Nothing marks you as anybody's agent, nothing appears on your sheet, and no line says what you have just helped along: the world simply moves a little further in the direction the thing you are holding wants. Breaking somebody's supply line pushes that same trouble back. Feeding it and starving it are the same ledger, read from two ends, and the only way to know which end you are on is to work it out.

entries.title: Somebody nobody has met is out there getting further away
entries.summary: A fourth world-scale trouble: roads that take a day longer than they did, and a milestone whose count will not come down.
entries.detail: A road that took four days takes five. A milestone reads the same distance however far you walk toward it, and nobody can say when that started. Untended, places stop being reachable at all — not walled off, just further every time you try. Two of the eleven artifacts feed it, and one of them is a map with a single road on it.

entries.title: The worst places in the world are finally allowed to say so
entries.summary: Sixteen places were written as worse than deadly and the game read every one of them as merely deadly. There is a sixth rung now.
entries.detail: The Maw, the Unlit Deep, the Wellspring Deep, the Long Grey and a dozen more were authored at the top of the scale on purpose, and the scale stopped one step below them — so the worst ground in the world looked exactly like ordinary deadly ground, wore the same colour on the map and carried the same word on its chip. It has its own rung, its own word and its own mark now. Legendary creatures walk only there, and rarely; the very worst things are still met through a story that goes looking for them, never by wandering. ⛑ Nothing about the other hundred and twenty-seven places changed.

entries.title: What a ruin can hold follows the ground it is on
entries.summary: A relic found on ordinary deadly ground is now the work of a great figure rather than a legendary one — a legend's work turns up only on the worst ground in the world.
entries.detail: The ceiling on what a found thing can have been made at rides the same ladder the creatures climb, so moving the top rung moved this with it. Anything that came from a named person is unaffected: their own standing is the honest number, and it arrived with a name attached.

entries.title: Some things are not to be beaten down
entries.summary: A creature with an old story about it can now be met as a problem to solve rather than a fight to win — the same creature, a different kind of encounter.
entries.detail: The tales carry remedies, and a remedy is a way through. So a creature the stories know can arrive as the situation it is, with a way through that is not swinging at it — and the game will not tell you what the way is unless you have earned it. ⛑ You meet these creatures exactly as often as before: the encounter is split between the fight and the way through, not added on top. It also fixes something measurable: with the full roster in, a character who talks rather than fights was down to three non-combat encounters where they used to have eleven. They have eleven again.

entries.title: Breaking somebody's carrier starves what they were carrying for
entries.summary: Four powers in the world quietly move something on somebody else's behalf. Finish one, or take its ground, and the thing it was feeding loses ground too.
entries.detail: You will not be told what it was feeding — that stays something you work out. What you get is the plain fact: they are finished, and something that was being carried through them is not being carried any more. The trouble they were feeding recedes, and everything that follows from how far along that trouble is follows from that: what the world says about it, and whether the thing at the end of it is close enough to arrive. Nothing is counted separately; the ground it loses IS the change.

entries.title: How far a broken line sets a hunger back is now a number you can turn
entries.summary: Breaking a carrier outright, taking one of its holds, turning it, or killing the one who led it — each is worth a stated amount, authored beside the other world dials.
entries.detail: Breaking is worth a whole step because a broken power stays broken until something puts it back; taking one of its holds is worth half, because ground can be retaken. The numbers sit with the rest of the world-simulation dials rather than in the engine, so they can be tuned without touching code. One of the four — killing the leader — is authored and not yet spent: no part of the game currently knows both a person's death and the power they led.

entries.title: Small wrong things, and what they add up to
entries.summary: Eighteen details are now out there to notice — a coin worn smooth, a bed still warm in an empty house, a street where every shutter came down and nobody decided to. Each has a perfectly ordinary explanation.
entries.detail: A guild's sun-mark. Old coin. A lodger. A lullaby. Every one of them is exactly the sort of thing you shrug at, and that is the point: nothing here is labelled a clue. Notice two of the same sort on one power's roads and the game will say you have seen this before. Notice three and it will tell you that something beyond that power is being fed, and that the power is how. What it will never do is tell you what is being fed — that comes from somebody who knows, or from the thing itself when it turns up. ⛑ And the marks are the same in every game: what you learn once, you recognise again.

entries.title: The same mark, two hundred miles away
entries.summary: Find one detail through two different powers in two different regions and the game says so — nobody in either place has heard of the other.
entries.detail: This is the one that cannot have an innocent explanation, and it takes no local proof at all: one mark, two powers, two regions. The reading is the same hand in both places, which is a very different thing from two towns having the same habit.

entries.title: What the world says about a trouble depends on what you have worked out
entries.summary: Confirm that a power is feeding something and the world starts naming that power when it talks about the trouble it feeds.
entries.detail: The three world-scale hungers each say three different things. Everybody gets the plain description of what is happening. Once your own collecting has confirmed which power is a supply line, the world starts saying where the answers are coming through — by name. Only knowing the name of the thing at the end of the line unlocks the last layer, and that never comes from the narrator.

entries.title: The world tells you what is going wrong before it tells you whose fault it is
entries.summary: Three new world-scale troubles are turning, and each one says a different thing depending on how much you have worked out.
entries.detail: Bargains that cannot be taken back. A light that is offered as safety and does not switch off. Houses getting quieter. Each of the three is a thing you can see happening long before anybody can tell you who benefits from it — and each has its own clock, so they do not arrive together. Work out which power is feeding one and the world starts naming that power. Learn whose hunger is behind it and the world starts saying that too. Until then, what you get is what everybody gets: the weather, honestly described.

entries.title: An arc shows a reading, not a number
entries.summary: The World tab printed “stage 2/4” beside a trouble's name, which told you how much of somebody's story was left before you knew there was a story.
entries.detail: Every stage of every world trouble has a name — Hard Bargains, Scouring Light, Empty Houses — and those names are the point: they say what is happening now. The count beside them was the machine keeping score where the reading should be, and it gave away that there was a fixed length to something you had not been told existed. It is gone, in the tab and in the two places a number could have crept back in. Which way a trouble is moving still shows, in words.

entries.title: Three of the great powers could never actually arrive
entries.summary: The things that arrive at the end of a world-scale story were stored in a shape nothing could read, shared one clock between two of them, or had no arrival at all.
entries.detail: One of them kept its two forms as a list where the engine looks for a pair, so it had no forms at all as far as the game was concerned. Two more shared a single story, which meant they would have arrived on the same day. One had no arrival written. All three have their own story now, and the shapes match what reads them — the original text is kept beside the corrected one, not replaced.

entries.title: A raid has somebody behind it
entries.summary: Raids on your holdings were always anonymous, even where a named power holds the ground — the game knew who was coming and never told the raid.
entries.detail: Whoever holds the ground around a place was meant to be the one who comes for what you keep there: their people, their captain, and a watch that can read who is coming rather than guess. All of it was built, and one missing word meant the raid never received the name — so every raid in the game was a faceless mob. It has a name now, where a power claims that ground, and the fifteen places in the world where one does are the ones where you will see it.

entries.title: A raid leader leads, and does not slaughter
entries.summary: A power's captain rides with its raids and is felt three ways — none of them winning the fight single-handed.
entries.detail: A leader belongs on the field, but a raid is not a conquest. So: while they stand, their people fight a step better — the same step whether they are a local captain or a legend, because what makes a legend matters elsewhere. If anyone stands for your place, the two of them meet: that is where the difference between a great captain and a hired hand is actually felt, and the loser's side gives ground. Your defender is hurt, not killed, and a cruel power will take one thing more on an overrun. Measured before it shipped: a hold that used to win about half its raids now wins about a third of them, where dropping the leader in as one more soldier had taken it to under a fifth.

entries.title: Your watch can take a captain alive
entries.summary: A raid leader whose raid is routed may be held rather than simply gone — and what happens next is yours.
entries.detail: A named leader is never killed off-screen in a raid you were not present at: that should be a scene you are in, not a line in a report. But break their raid and your watch may be holding them. It shows up on your Holdings screen: who you have, who they led, and the day they were taken. Ransom, a bargain, a trial — that is a story to play. Or you can let them go, and the power that sent them will think better of you for it.

entries.title: A creature belongs somewhere
entries.summary: What can find you now depends on where you are standing — dark places, water, ruins, high ground — instead of everything being possible everywhere.
entries.detail: Every creature can now say where it belongs, by terrain and by whose land it is, and the encounter picker reads it. So a thing that lives in the dark rises in the dark and a thing that sings over water sings over water. Measured before it shipped: one place in the world has nothing at all that can find it there, and it is the safest inn on the map. Anything that does not say where it belongs is still possible anywhere, which is every creature in the game before this.

entries.title: There is a way through, and the old stories know it
entries.summary: Creatures made from a people's folklore carry the remedy from the tale — and the remedy is true.
entries.detail: The Storm made each people's stories real in their own lands, remedies and all: a light the thing cannot come at you through, a mirror it cannot look into, running water it will not cross, a toll it will take instead of your life. If your own people tell the tale, you have it from the first look. If they don't, you can work it out — read the thing rather than swing at it, and a success gives you the tale for good. Act on it and it works: the thing is ended, avoided or turned as the story says, and nobody has to out-fight it. It stays on your encounter panel once you know it, so it doesn't scroll away with the moment you learned it.

entries.title: The ones who protect can fight back
entries.summary: A body whose whole purpose is guarding people could not answer an attack at all, so the same five of them lost people every season and never once gained any.
entries.detail: What a power does each pass had consequences for some verbs and none for others: pushing outward and recruiting made a force stronger, feuding ground both sides down — and protecting, patrolling and taxing did nothing at all. So a body that attacks rotates its wins against its own losses and comes out even, while a body that guards takes every loss and answers none. Guarding a line now HOLDS it: a loss that has not yet landed is cancelled. It is not a victory and it grows nobody — the line simply held.

entries.title: Nothing in the world is ground to nothing any more
entries.summary: A force could be worn from full strength down to a single soldier inside a year, because the world let strength fall four times faster than it could rise.
entries.detail: A force may visibly grow about four times a year, on purpose: reaching your full size should take years rather than a fortnight. Losing had no such limit, so anyone in a long war was destroyed — measured over five years, five of them went from their full strength to one soldier left. Losing is now paced the same way growing is. A war is a grind that neither side wins quickly instead of a countdown to somebody's annihilation, and what YOU do to a power is not slowed by this at all: your own fighting counts the moment it happens.

entries.title: Champions go out, and orders carry the war
entries.summary: Two new things a power can do: send a champion out on a quest, and carry the fight to whoever has been fighting it.
entries.detail: A power can now send its champion out — they come back with renown, a relic or fresh hands, and the news says so. And it can carry the war: every foe takes losses, and the news names who did it. A crusader's foes are the ones it names as rivals AND anyone who names it as one, so whoever has been feuding you is exactly who you can answer. A crusade by the strong costs them nothing; a crusade by the weak against something larger costs them too, which is a war they chose.

entries.title: The world knows a person's name even when you don't
entries.summary: Someone you have met but not been introduced to is no longer written into the shared world under the description you know them by.
entries.detail: A person passes into the shared world once enough travelers have met them, and the name it publishes is meant to be the one the world knows — not the placeholder any single traveler is stuck with. Two halves of that record were built and the wrong half won, so a woman whose name is Vail Langley entered the world as "Enforcer of Seraphine's will", which is only what Loki calls her because nobody has told him yet. She is published under her own name now, and he still has to learn it.

entries.title: The world has things in it that can kill anyone
entries.summary: What you can meet on the road now climbs all the way to the top of the world, instead of stopping at the eleventh rung of a hundred.
entries.detail: Every creature you could run into was drawn from the bottom of the ladder — the hardest thing the world would put in front of you unasked sat at about level eleven, and a character past that point was walking through a world that could no longer reach them. The ladder now runs to the top: a quiet road still holds the small things, and the far dangerous ground holds what belongs there. The very worst of them are not met by wandering into them — they are met through a story that goes looking.

entries.title: A quiet road stays quiet
entries.summary: Raising the ladder would have put a leader on a farm track, so what each grade of danger is allowed to send has moved down one step to match.
entries.detail: Measured before it shipped: on the safest ground a level-10 character was already meeting something at level eleven, and lifting the ladder underneath that would have made a roadside walk lethal. So the gate moved rather than the ladder — danger 1 sends what danger 1 should send. On the safest ground you now meet something a little below you instead of a little above; the change is felt at the top end, where the hardest ground finally has something hard on it.

entries.title: A legend's things can become yours
entries.summary: Something taken from a named person — a crown from a hall, a blade off a body — now carries who it was and what they could do with it.
entries.detail: The great items in this world are the ones somebody great carried, and until now taking one gave you an ordinary object with a nice description. A thing that comes from a named person now remembers them, and what it can grow into is measured from THEIR standing, not yours — a master's work is strong in an apprentice's hand. It arrives with no powers of its own and earns them through use, which is what makes a found crown worth carrying rather than a finished weapon. It also leaves their hands for good: the same crown cannot be handed to you twice.

entries.title: What a ruin can hold is bounded by the ruin
entries.summary: A relic found in a roadside ruin can no longer have been made by someone at the top of the world.
entries.detail: An item's making can now be stated, which is what lets a legend's gear be strong — and left open, it would let a quiet ruin hand out the best thing in the world. Where a thing has no person behind it, the ground it was found on sets the ceiling, on the same ladder the creatures climb. Anything that came from a named person is not bounded this way: their own standing is the honest number, and it arrived with a name attached.

entries.title: The map will take you anywhere there is a way
entries.summary: A place you can reach by a route — not only one road away — now offers to plan the journey, instead of saying it isn't connected.
entries.detail: The map would only offer travel to a place directly joined to the one you stand in, which is about three places out of a hundred and forty-three. Everywhere else read "not directly reachable", even though the world is all one piece and the game could already lay a route to almost any of it. Pick a far place now and it offers to plan the journey, with the days it will take. Only somewhere nothing can reach is refused — and that refusal still names a neighbour to go by way of.

entries.title: You were standing in someone else's world
entries.summary: A character could end up recorded at a place that exists only on another character's save — and then nothing on the map was reachable.
entries.detail: Places you grow in play were being merged into the world and left there when you switched characters, so a second character could be moved to a place the first one had found. On the next load that place was gone from their world, and with it every road out: the map said nothing was connected because, for them, nothing was. Each character's grown world is now put away when another takes over, and a character already recorded somewhere their own map does not have is moved to a place they do know.

entries.title: A ship is not a place to sail to
entries.summary: A holding that moves was offering itself as a destination, a day away.
entries.detail: The list of places to sail for excluded where she lies, but not what she is — so a hold that is also a place on the map offered itself. It now leaves out where she lies, anywhere that is one of your own holdings, and anywhere carrying her own name; and the list is sorted by how far, nearest first, with what she cannot reach at the bottom.

entries.title: Everyone who walks with you is on the list
entries.summary: People who joined you in the story were being dropped from your party screen — one save showed one of the four travelling with him.
entries.detail: When the story added someone to your side, it sometimes filed them under a name the rest of the game did not recognise, and the party screen quietly left them out. Those records are repaired when you next load, and the screen now shows everyone travelling with you — including a companion with no crafts written down, who could never be shown before. They stand in the line whether or not the engine has anything to say about what they can do.

entries.title: Ask someone to walk with you
entries.summary: The Party screen can now ask anyone you know to travel with you — it had no way to add anybody at all.
entries.detail: Until now the only routes into your party were the story adding somebody, or raising a band — and a band needs three people under your command or two holdings, so a player with neither had no way in. There is a button on the Party screen now: everyone you know who would come, searchable, with what they are and how close you stand. Closeness still decides who can be brought FORWARD — a named place, a stance, a preferred craft — and anyone who will come can travel with you and stand in the line.

entries.title: You are not blamed for other people's wars
entries.summary: The news was telling you that you had killed people who died in a feud between two powers you had never fought.
entries.detail: Powers grind each other down in the background — that is what a feud is. The game recorded those deaths in the same place it records the people YOU kill, so it went on to tell you that a power had taken an interest in you because you had killed dozens of theirs, when you had killed none. Those two are counted apart now, the grudges raised on the mistake are withdrawn when you next load, and a power with a real reason to notice you will still notice. The news about a feud also says whose feud it is.

entries.title: The people who defend your places fight like themselves
entries.summary: A defender now brings the same crafts to a raid that they would bring to a duel — twelve of the fifteen people standing on a hold across every save, where before it was one.
entries.detail: Everyone in this world has crafts, whether or not anyone wrote them down: the game draws them from the three domains a person stands in, the same way it draws their level and their energy. A one-on-one fight has always used that draw. A raid on one of your places did not — it read only the crafts somebody had typed onto the record, which for almost everyone is none, so your wardens met raiders as bodies with no skills. They fight as themselves now.

entries.title: It matters who is standing there
entries.summary: A defender with a craft that reaches several people now counts for more than a body in a raid — until their energy for it runs out.
entries.detail: A raid used to be decided by weight of numbers: thirteen raiders beat three wardens, a lone epic, even a lone mythic, every time, because a defender whose craft strikes six people was counted exactly like one who throws a punch. Now a named figure's craft counts. Someone who can reach six is worth more than one sword — capped by how many are actually coming, so six targets against three raiders is three. A craft that guards absorbs the line's first losses, one that heartens the people around them lifts a whole watch a rung, and ordinary hands fight as they always did. And it costs energy: a clash runs several exchanges, and a defender who spends everything on the first rush fights the rest of it plainly. The report of the raid now says who made the difference.

entries.title: A thing is as strong as the hand that made it
entries.summary: An item now carries the level it was made at, and what it can hold is read from that — so a master's artifact is strong in an apprentice's hand.
entries.detail: Until now an item's power was read from whoever was holding it, so an artifact a level-80 master forged was indistinguishable from a level-40 one, and past about level 40 nothing rose at all. An item now remembers the level it was made at, and the ceiling reads whichever is higher — the item's or yours. It never reads lower: your own skill still counts. Items made below level 40 are untouched, and what you can actually DO with a master's work is still your own rolls and your own energy. Work made above 40 keeps climbing: a seventh power opens on items made at 60, an eighth at 85.

entries.title: Your places, arranged by what you came to do
entries.summary: The Holdings screen is a line for your whole estate, a card per place that only reads, and a page per place with six tabs.
entries.detail: The top line says how many places you hold, what they do to your purse each pass, and what wants your attention — and each warning is a link straight to the place it means, on the tab that answers it. A card below shows the picture, the name, three numbers (people, per pass, how it fares) and one thing worth knowing; it no longer carries a dozen selects and buttons, so on a phone it is one row high. Opening a place gives it its own page, with Overview, People, Build, Store & money, Attack & Defense and Records — and every action lives on the tab whose job it is. An action that needs you standing there is now greyed and says so, instead of silently vanishing when you are elsewhere. Nothing about how a place works has changed; what changed is that you can find it.

entries.title: A place remembers, and now it will tell you
entries.summary: Every condition change and every event a place has lived through is written down, and the Records tab shows it.
entries.detail: A holding's history has been recorded since holdings existed — raids, a keeper appointed, a feature built, a season that went badly — and no screen had ever shown it. The Records tab lists it newest first, with the day.

entries.title: The estate panel valued every place as if the ground were the same
entries.summary: A holding on rich or poor ground is now worth what its ground makes it worth, on every screen that says a number.
entries.detail: Four different screens asked the engine what a place earns, and each asked slightly differently: some told it what ground the place stands on and some did not, and one did not say whose place it was, which is what pays a relay station's runner fees. So the world screen's estate panel could show a figure the place would never pay. Every screen now asks the same question through one call, so two screens cannot quietly answer differently.

entries.title: The Holdings screen on a phone
entries.summary: A place's card is now about half the height it was at phone width, and the build costs no longer run off the edge of the screen.
entries.detail: Measured at 375 pixels wide: a card's summary line could run to ten lines on its own, making the card 319 pixels tall where the design asks for one row — it now shows two lines, with the whole sentence on hover. And on the Build tab, eight of the eleven build costs sat off the right edge of the sheet with no way to scroll to them; the list wraps now, and a quantity never splits from what it is a quantity of.

entries.title: A short walk stops being offered as a five-week journey
entries.summary: A place three hours away was being planned as a 36-day trek through a distant gate. Where the ground between two places is under a day's walk, it is a step — you simply go.
entries.detail: A holding another traveller founded brings its own roads with it when it arrives in your world, and those roads lead back to THEIR neighbours. The planner was following them. The ground itself is now the arbiter: a road may honestly be longer than the crow flies — a chasm, a river, a mountain — but it cannot turn a three-hour walk into a five-week one.

entries.title: The rations you bought are rations
entries.summary: Food for the road only counted if it was the one item the rules named. Anything you actually bought — road rations, trail provisions, a waystation bundle — read as nothing, and a journey told you that you carried none.
entries.detail: Five of the six road provisions in the game were invisible. Food is recognised for what it is now, and a bundle that names its own days is worth them: two four-day bundles is eight days of eating, not two.

entries.title: The estate line shows up
entries.summary: The one-line summary of all your holdings was being worked out and then not drawn.
entries.detail: A number computed and never shown is the same as no number.

entries.title: Your holdings, arranged by what you came to do
entries.summary: A strip at the top reads your whole estate in one line — how many places, what they do to your purse each pass, and what wants your attention, with every alert a link to the place it means. Each place then opens as its own page with tabs: Overview, People, Build, Store & money, Defence, Records.
entries.detail: The screen had grown to carry thirty-three different actions interleaved with everything you read, so neither worked. Reading and doing are now separated the way they already were inside the manage panel, and the doing is grouped by the job you opened the place to do.

entries.title: A place remembers, and now it will tell you
entries.summary: The Records tab shows what has happened at a holding — every change of condition, every raid, every keeper appointed — newest first.
entries.detail: The engine has written that history since holdings existed and no screen had ever shown it.

entries.title: The watch and the walls show even when the store is empty
entries.summary: What a place can hold off, who stands watch, and what a raid would risk were all hidden unless the place had goods in store.
entries.detail: They were drawn inside a block that only ran when the store had something in it — so a bare place, which is exactly when you most want to know what defends it, showed nothing at all.

entries.title: The GM stops re-telling the beat you just read
entries.summary: It is shown the last few beats in full so it knows where the scene stands — and it is now told plainly that this is not permission to say them again.
entries.detail: Nothing had ever told it otherwise. It now starts from what has CHANGED since the last beat: no re-describing the room, no re-introducing people already standing there, no opening paragraph that sums up what you just read.

entries.title: A place you are standing in keeps its picture
entries.summary: The scene picture was being drawn again every single beat you spent somewhere — ten beats in one shop was ten new pictures of that shop. It now shows the picture the place already has, and draws one only when there is none.
entries.detail: The picture was seeded on the GM's description of THIS moment, so every beat was a new seed and a new drawing. It now takes what the place already has, in the usual order: the one you chose, the world's, the authored one, then the one drawn for you. Drawing it again is still a button, whenever you want this particular moment.

entries.title: Learning someone's name finds the person, instead of making a second one
entries.summary: Somebody you had met but could not yet name was being recorded twice — once under what you called them, and again the moment the story said their real name.
entries.detail: A person carries their true name from the moment they exist, held back until the fiction reveals it. The part of the game that decides whether someone is already known had never read that field, so a revealed name matched nobody and started a fresh record — with the old one keeping the history, the standing and the face.

entries.title: Adding someone to your party actually adds them
entries.summary: If the GM agrees to bring someone along, it lands — even when the story has been calling them something other than the name they were first written down under. And if nobody in the world matches, they are written down rather than dropped.
entries.detail: A join used to take the name it was given at face value, so asking for somebody registered under an earlier label did nothing at all, silently. Three people already travelling with characters had no record of themselves for this reason.

entries.title: A keeper who stops travelling with you does not lose their post
entries.summary: Appointing somebody to keep a holding is exactly why they stop walking at your side — and the world was reading that as them abandoning it, every single pass.
entries.detail: A castellan stays at the castle while you walk away. Someone genuinely gone — dead, or departed — still leaves the post behind, which is what that rule was there for.

entries.title: Work above level 60 is finally paid as what it is
entries.summary: A job could not be pitched above level 60, and a job's level is what its crystal, its experience and its danger all scale from — so past that point your work was quietly priced as a level-60's.
entries.detail: Levels run to 100. Everything that reads one now carries the whole way, and the game checks it by driving a level-100 person through every reader rather than hunting for the number in the code.

entries.title: The people on your wall fight as themselves
entries.summary: A march-warden on your gate now meets a raid as a warden; a filtration engineer standing the same watch meets it as what he is. Before this, every named defender in the game fought at the lowest quality there is.
entries.detail: What they are worth comes from the standing they have earned and from what their own record says they do, and it is the same number the card shows you before the raid ever comes.

entries.title: Anyone who walks with you is in your party
entries.summary: If the story sends someone along, they are on your party list from that moment — and they are in your fights, helping as they are able, or hanging back behind you. What closeness earns is a NAMED PLACE: a stance you set, a craft you star, a turn of their own.
entries.detail: Until now someone had to be an ally or better before the game would record that they travelled with you, so people the story clearly sent along simply were not there. Being close to someone now buys them a place at the front of your line rather than permission to walk beside you — and someone who has sworn to you comes forward whatever their standing.

entries.title: Name your band when you name it — they answer when you have earned them
entries.summary: If you give your people a name in a scene, they are your band from that moment and they appear on the Bands tab. Whether they can be called, sent or posted is a separate thing, and the tab says plainly what it would take.
entries.detail: Naming a band used to be refused outright unless you already led enough people, so a name spoken in the story went into your deeds and your codex and nowhere else — and nothing said why. A band you have named now stands in your record and keeps its name, marked as not yet answering, exactly as a legion can be formed before it can be wielded.

entries.title: A raid has somebody leading it, and your watch can tell who
entries.summary: When a power comes for one of your holds, its captain comes with it — by name. The watch reads who that is: someone whose whole trade is arriving unnoticed is harder to spot than a column of toll-men.
entries.detail: Until now the other side of a raid was a count and a description, so your watch had nothing to read and the fight had nobody in it with a name. The raid record now says who led it. Whether that captain also takes the field is a setting, and it is off for the moment — a leader swinging changes who wins a raid a great deal, and that is a decision to make deliberately rather than discover.

entries.title: Who you post on the watch counts for who they are
entries.summary: A seasoned warden on the wall is worth several willing hands, and a filtration engineer standing the same watch is worth what he is — present, and not a lookout. The card names the rung and the reason beside each number.
entries.detail: Every person in the game already has a standing worked out from what they have done and what their record says of them. The watch was not reading it, so everyone counted the same. Now the watch says, for instance, "Siol leads the watch — leader, their own record says they do this", and what you are shown is what a raid actually pays.

entries.title: The risk shown on a hold is the risk the world pays
entries.summary: A keeper's standing and a watcher's standing are read from the whole person, the same way the world reads them when the days pass.
entries.detail: The hold screen was reading only what you personally had written down about someone, while the world read everything known about them. For about a quarter of people those come out differently — sometimes by a great deal — so a hold could show you one raid risk and then quietly settle a different one.

entries.title: Whether the watch sees them is now a contest, not a headcount
entries.summary: One good captain on the wall is worth more than four tired hands, and twelve burglars are harder to spot than twelve household guard. The card shows both sides — what your side is looking with, what theirs is coming with — and what one more hand would actually add.
entries.detail: Before this, anybody on watch meant every raid was seen and nobody meant none ever was. Now the people standing there count for who they are, the things that watch count for what they are, and the party coming counts for who IT is rather than for how rough the ground is. Nothing changes at the bottom: with nobody on watch, a raid here is still never seen.

entries.title: Reaching for your own dead is rolled, and you see the odds first
entries.summary: The chance of bringing someone back is shown before you reach, with every reason it is what it is — how deep they have sunk, your craft, what you were to them, whether they promised to come for you.
entries.detail: Straining past your craft reaches a depth you otherwise could not, and it is a strain: it lowers the odds rather than raising them. A failure still sinks them a depth, and at the deep dark it still seals them, so the deep dark remains a gamble worth being afraid of.

entries.title: Someone who refused to be brought back is left in peace
entries.summary: If the dead said they did not want to come back, no reach for them rolls at all — whatever the bond, whatever the craft.
entries.detail: The refusal was honoured when deciding whether a friend would volunteer to go after you, and not when the reach itself was settled. It is honoured in both places now, and asking costs nothing: nobody sinks for having been asked.

entries.title: A holding tells you what it can hold off, send out, and who else stands on its ground
entries.summary: Every wall, ward and watch with what it gives you and what the next level would cost — in goods, and in upkeep. Beside it: how many more hands you could raise here, and which powers reach this place and whether they make it harder or quieter.
entries.detail: A rung you cannot price is not a decision, so each one says its effect, its price, what the keep becomes, and plainly why the store cannot pay for it yet. “Raise from here” takes you to the Bands tab rather than being a second way to raise a band.

entries.title: Maintenance
Maintenance
Bringing someone back is a roll now, and you can see the odds
entries.summary: Reaching for the dead was pass-or-fail by the GM's word. It has a number: how deep they have gone, how far your craft reaches past it, what you were to them, and whether somebody is holding the way open.
entries.detail: Being told “that is past your reach” is still free and still costs them nothing — the roll happens only when you CAN get that deep, and that is the costly path: a failure sinks them a depth, and a failure at the deep dark seals them. So the threshold is a near-certainty for someone who loved you and the deep dark is a real gamble. The odds show on the who-comes-for-you block per depth, and they are the odds the engine rolls.

entries.title: A watch can miss them
entries.summary: A raid used to be seen if anybody at all stood watch. Now the watch rolls: bodies on the wall, things that watch, against how rough the ground the raiders came off.
entries.detail: Nobody watching is still never seen — an empty wall does not get lucky. Past a handful of bodies, another one honestly adds nothing to SEEING them, and the card says so rather than pretending: they add to the fight that follows. The holding card shows the chance, what built it, and what one more body would be worth. And the record now says whether the watch missed them or nobody was there, which are two different failures.

entries.title: The version in the address bar is gone rather than wrong
entries.summary: A cache-busting stamp from an old forced reload sat in the URL looking like a version that had stopped incrementing.
entries.detail: It was never a version — it is written once when a new build reloads a tab, and it had done its job by the time you saw it. It is cleared on boot now; every other part of the address is left alone.

entries.title: Maintenance
Maintenance
Every feature says what it is, what it does, and what it is for
entries.summary: A hold's features are grouped by what they're for — defence, watch, production, craft, community, market, travel, meaning — and each one carries a plain line about what it is and a line of flavour, with its real numbers beside them.
entries.detail: The numbers are composed from the feature's own fields rather than written into the words, so a wall that starts adding 2 to your defence says 2 the same day the rule changes.

entries.title: See every way the store can leave, priced side by side
entries.summary: Selling it yourself, letting the keeper work through it, or sending a caravan — each with what it gets, how long it takes, and what it returns per pass. Beside it: what a raid would take at this stock, and how often one gets through.
entries.detail: The comparison is ranked on what each way returns PER PASS, because the clock is the cost that dominates: a haul that fetches three times the price can take fifty passes and net a twentieth as much as selling where you stand. The raid line names which things are costing you — the ground, how full the store is, whether it is guarded, who keeps it — so a walled hold under a good keeper visibly earns the right to stock up.

entries.title: Building something with a craft costs that craft's energy
entries.summary: Raising a wall with a ward now costs what putting that ward to the place would cost any other way, shown on the option before you pick it. Plain work — goods and labour, no craft named — is unchanged.
entries.detail: Applying a craft to a hold through 'Apply a craft' already cost its energy; through 'Build' it was free, which made building the cheaper way to get the same thing.

entries.title: Maintenance
Maintenance
Maintenance
Who comes for you — and whether they have actually said so
entries.summary: The death block is now three answers per person, kept apart: can they reach you, would they bother, and have they said they will. Someone who made that promise in a scene is recorded, named, and shown with the words they used.
entries.detail: It used to end with “that is a conversation to have with them, not a setting” — and kept saying it after the conversation had happened, because it was reading the bond and a bond is not a promise. A pledge is its own record now, written by the GM from the scene it was made in, never inferred from closeness and never quietly removed: taking one back is spoken out loud. If nobody has promised, the block says so and puts an Ask button beside the people who could. Reach is shown as can/can’t at each depth — no percentage, because nothing rolls one yet.

entries.title: The tear-down button works on something still being built
entries.summary: Pressing × on a feature under construction did nothing at all and said nothing.
entries.detail: The buttons were numbered from one list of a hold’s features and the removal looked that number up in another — the two agree only while nothing is under construction, and a feature you pay for starts under construction. The same mismatch would have silently deleted every build in progress when you tore down a finished one. Stopping work on an unfinished build now says that is what it is, rather than calling it a tear-down.

entries.title: Say which craft raised a hold's feature — and it lasts accordingly
entries.summary: When you build something at a holding, you can now name the craft you used. A craft that makes or mends stands permanently; one that wards or defends lasts a season, warns you a pass before it goes, and can be renewed.
entries.detail: A feature record has carried a `craftIds` field since the day features arrived, and it was empty on every feature of every character — because the only door that could fill it was the GM's, and the door a player uses, standing there having just cast the thing, had no way to say so. The duration rule was already written and only the 'apply a craft to the place' path could reach it; both paths read the one rule now, the seasonal pass warns and lapses a crafted feature exactly as it does a crafted improvement, and the ↻ Refresh button takes it by the feature's name or by the craft's.

entries.title: A character who cannot harm keeps a plain strike
entries.summary: If none of your crafts can hit for free, you get fists again — and if none of them can block for free, you get a guard. The two are decided separately now.
entries.detail: The rule that retires the universal fallbacks used to ask one question of your whole kit and withdraw both answers on one yes. A Reader whose free moves are all reads lost the bare strike as well and had no way to act at all. Measured on the saved characters: two of fourteen had no harming move whatsoever, and four more gain a free way to hit or block when their energy runs dry. They are still not crafts — they cannot be learned, practised, aspired to, or offered as a job skill, and they do not make a Reader count as a fighter.

entries.title: Maintenance
A round you won outright is no longer reported as a draw
entries.summary: Driving an opponent back is the most decisive thing that can happen in a round — and the line under the fight was calling those rounds "neither gains — it's even", or sometimes crediting them to the other side.
entries.detail: Filling the momentum meter drives the losing side back and then RESETS the meter, so they are still in the fight. The receipt worked out who won by comparing the meter before and after — and the reset had already put it back. Across a simulated 2,410 rounds, 903 of them were rounds like this. The receipt now reads the drive-back itself, names it, and counts it toward the break; the meter line shows where the meter actually reached before it reset.

entries.title: The “driven back” counter showed a number the fight was not using
entries.summary: The header said 2, and a level-20 opponent takes up to 10. You could fill the pips and watch the fight carry on.
entries.detail: How many times a side must be driven back has scaled with their level since September — half their level, capped at 10, and easing by one for every two rounds you have fought. Three places in the interface were still reading the old flat number. They all ask the engine now. The pips are gone with it: one count, in words, because ten diamonds is not a thing anyone reads.

entries.title: A read is no longer described as a blow
entries.summary: Read someone with a sensing craft and the line said “your blow is turned aside” — in the same sentence that had just said you read them.
entries.detail: The sentence describing how two moves met knew only whether each was defensive. A read is neither defensive nor an attack, so it was filed as an attack and got an attack's words. Sensing verbs have their own now, in every kind: a fight, a standoff and a chase each describe being read in their own terms.

entries.title: You can see what they are about to do, and what in your kit answers it
entries.summary: Once you have read an opponent, the fight names the move they are set to make, why they are making it, and which of your crafts makes it hardest for them.
entries.detail: The old line welded a fact about the round that had just happened onto the words “gathering to”, which is the future — so it read as nonsense. The two are separated: what they last did is labelled as the past, and what they are set to do is computed from the same deterministic policy the fight itself will use. It only shows once your choice can no longer change it, so it is never a guess.

entries.title: The roll breakdown knows whose roll it is
entries.summary: Opening an opponent's roll used to show their numbers under “your base” and “your own d100”.
entries.detail: One panel drew both rolls and had no idea which it was showing. It names the side now, and uses their name. It also says plainly whether the roll succeeded or failed instead of whether it “landed”, and both percentages on screen say which question they answer — the roll's own chance, and the move card's chance of beating the other side.

entries.title: Enter sends a move you have typed into a fight
entries.summary: The box where you shape a step in your own words had no Enter key — you had to find the button.

entries.title: The momentum bar says what it is worth
entries.summary: It now shows the bonus it is giving your rolls right now, and names its one real landmark: fill it and they are driven back.
entries.detail: Momentum is a roll modifier, not the way a fight ends — that is the drive-back counter. The bar was a bare percentage with no way to learn either fact.

entries.title: The finisher note names the craft, or says nothing
entries.summary: It used to announce that a decisive finisher “could end this in one beat” without saying which of your crafts could do it.

entries.title: The ✦ Rich button has left the input row
entries.summary: ✦ Tell it again, richer does the same job after a beat, where you can see whether it is worth it. The default still lives in Settings.

entries.title: The dev hero has a kit to match his level
entries.detail: The dev test scenarios lifted the hero to level 20 for the command slots and left him with two crafts, neither of which could harm — and R47 retires the universal fallback strike for anyone whose own crafts carry a free floor, so there was no way to attack at all. The scenarios now learn a spread through `learnAbility`, gates and all, and report what refused.

entries.title: Three fights you can set up from the dev screen
entries.summary: The Legs screen can now stage a band clash, a legion field and a full-party fight, so the three newest combat surfaces can be played without waiting for the story to offer one.
entries.detail: Dev apparatus only — no player meets it. Each scenario lifts the earned inputs (level, presence) rather than bypassing the gates, so what you see is the real ladder doing the real thing.

entries.title: Somebody is coming for you
entries.summary: Your character now has one figure whose existence argues with what their story is about — and the world will not let them die while you are somewhere else.
entries.detail: It is chosen from what is already true about you: your own people carried to their pole, a force that would build over ground you hold, somebody in your company who stands against them, or a story that answers yours. They act on their own clock, whether or not you are looking, so what reaches you first is a rumour, a road built over, a letter, their name in somebody else’s mouth — not the person. You will not be told who they are until the story tells you. And if another traveller’s world kills them, here they are only wounded: that ending is yours to write or to lose.

entries.title: Nine more countries have someone holding them
entries.summary: Wardens, moots, courts and orders now hold ground in the Palelands, the Unmade, the Lattice Cities, the Descent, the Ascent, the Umbral Depths and the Deepwood — twenty-three of the world’s thirty-eight countries are held.
entries.detail: Among them: the Wardens of Cairnhold and the Harvest Hand pushing toward the Quiet Ground; the Masters of the Scour, who are asked before every ending they make, and the Scouring, which has stopped asking; a Grand Lattice waiting on a specification to be finished; a Hollow Court that keeps an empty chair and grants what the Mavens will not recognise; the Seraphic Orders with an Inquisition inside them; a Harborward that wants refuge in the dark and nothing else; and a Deepwood moot arguing about sealing the wood. Four of them are led by people you can meet, and the Descent and the Ascent are now set against each other.

entries.title: One High Luminary, not two
