entries.summary: The Master of the Radiant Plateau existed twice — as High Luminary Sera and as the High Luminary — and they were always the same person.
entries.detail: She is one record now: Seraphine Aurel Lumenhall, and “Sera” is what her own people call her. What each copy knew is kept, including what she knows about the falsified purity reports, which three quests turn on. If a quest of yours was given by the copy that went away, it now points at her — nothing you started is lost.

entries.title: Everyone has a whole name
entries.summary: People the world gives you now carry a first name, a family name of their own people, and a middle name behind it — where before they had a first name and an epithet.
entries.detail: A Marcher is a Brandt or a Voss; a Churnfolk is a Muddle or a Crankle; the Lattice counts its children and the Verists take virtues for middle names. There are a thousand new names behind this, and a family name now comes from the bearer’s own people instead of a short list shared by everybody — which is why you used to meet more than one of the same name. What you HEAR is still what people say aloud; the whole name sits behind it, and you can see it on their card.

entries.title: Six more countries have someone holding them
entries.summary: Nine forces now hold ground in the Radiant Wastes, the Somatic Reaches, the Quickwood, the Making, the Gearlands and the Numinous Reach — so whoever your people are, you have heard of somebody at home.
entries.detail: Among them: the zealots inside the Blaze and the lens-holders who keep the border against them; a temple of the body and the custody that keeps the ones Cogitants leave behind; a moot that has never decided anything in a hurry; builders who cannot stop, and the court where the best plan each season governs; a written specification for everything; and a choir that sings people gently out of their bodies. Three of them are led by people you can meet. Every character on this device now begins knowing forces in their own country rather than only the ones whose names travel.

entries.title: Your people is recognised again
entries.summary: A few older characters named a people the game had since renamed, so anything that asked where they were from got no answer at all.
entries.detail: It never showed as an error — it simply read as "no such people", and the game fell back to wherever you happened to be standing. Those characters are corrected on load, and they now hear of the forces that hold their own country.

entries.title: Your codex is no longer capped
entries.summary: It used to stop taking new subjects at sixty, and the next thing you learned was filed onto an unrelated entry. Now everything you learn about gets its own entry, however much you already know.
entries.detail: What handles a codex that fills up is the reading: once a subject has gathered enough facts, it earns a paragraph that states the whole of what is known, and the older facts move underneath it as evidence rather than crowding the page. The fuller your codex gets, the sooner and the more of it condenses — so it keeps getting easier to read as you learn more, instead of shutting. Nothing is ever deleted; the facts are kept under the reading.

entries.title: A heroic is weekly again
entries.summary: People of great standing were turning up far too often — a heroic every second day where the world is meant to offer one about weekly.
entries.detail: The cadence was stored per person rather than per rung, so when the cast was sorted onto its proper rungs and fifty-nine people became heroes, the world started offering one three times as often as it should. It is now set in the terms it was meant in — how many days between meeting one — and divided across however many such people the world holds, so adding more great figures makes each of them rarer instead of making the whole rung common. A market town still offers more than an empty moor.

entries.title: You have heard of them
entries.summary: Your codex now begins with the forces that hold ground — the ones in the country you started in and the ones your people is from, and the few whose names travel the whole world.
entries.detail: You have not met any of them. The entries say so, and each carries one plain line about who they are, which is what having heard of somebody amounts to. From there you can learn about them as you play without ever standing in front of one: what they want, what they hold, who they answer to. A force that takes an interest in you is one you have heard of from then on, whatever you knew an hour before. Knowing of a crown is still not knowing the man who wears it — he is a stranger until you meet him.

entries.title: Word reaches you about the ones you know of
entries.summary: News that a force has grown, or lost people it will not get back, no longer arrives about a name you have never heard.
entries.detail: It was a line about a stranger, and eleven strangers reporting their business is how a player learns to stop reading the world news. Now it comes about the forces you know of — which, from this update, is most of the ones near you.

entries.title: They have an opinion of you, and some of them come looking
entries.summary: Every force that holds ground now has a standing with you that moves on what you do to it — and when you cross one, settle near one, get rich, or befriend its rival, it takes an interest in you.
entries.detail: Kill a toll gang's men and they think worse of you; take their post and they think a great deal worse. It reads on the same scale as a people's or a town's opinion, and the reasons are kept, so you can see what decided it. A force that thinks well enough of you will field what it has beside you. And a force can now form an intention about you: each one is authored with what makes it notice — crossing it, holding ground near it, carrying real money, standing well with its rival — and when one of those is true it takes an interest, once, and wants from you exactly what its own record says it wants. If its leader is somebody you have met, they start looking for you. If not, the world knows and the story brings them; nobody you have never met is quietly added to the people you know.

entries.title: The forces holding the world act on their own
entries.summary: Each of the eleven powers now does one thing a pass — tolls, raids, taxes, feuds, sends tribute up the line — and over a season that shows: a crown its vassals keep paying grows, two rivals grinding each other down shrink.
entries.detail: The Switchback Tollmen and the Edge Riders both answer to the Gralloch Crown, and over a world year it is the Crown that gets stronger on what they send it. Two rivals who feud — the Slip and the Barony at Firstsight, the Radiant and Harmonic Councils — wear each other down instead. A force can only grow into what its kind can be, and it grows about once a season rather than in a fortnight. None of it is narrated unless something actually changed: over one year the pass is silent on 134 of 144 days, because a toll gang tolling is not news — you already feel it in the danger of the road. And people who belong to a force now only turn up where that force still stands: clear the Tollmen and their toll-bandits stop appearing on the switchback altogether, instead of the road producing them forever.

entries.title: Somebody holds the ground now
entries.summary: Eleven forces are in the world — a toll gang on the switchback, the Gralloch Crown, the Edge Riders, the Undercount under the markets, two rival coasts, the Ender's Host below the Marchward, and three councils. They raise the danger where they stand, they raid with a name, and twelve of their places can be taken.
entries.detail: Until now the world had no forces in it: a raid was a number, danger was whatever a place was authored at, and there was nobody on the other side of a battle. Eleven powers now hold ground. Where they stand the road reads more dangerous — the Gralloch and the Edge Riders together make Tumbledown Market as bad as it gets — and clearing them puts it back. A raid on your hold comes from that force's own people and the ones you kill stay dead. And twelve places they hold, from a chain-post above a waystation to the Feast Hall itself, can be assaulted by your band: take one and it becomes yours. Thirteen new people came with them, each with a whole name and, where they hold one, a title — Dessa Maerin Wyck, Harl Osric Maddock King of the Gralloch, Agathe Morrow Hesk Mother of the Undercount, Wenna Maud Dresh Councilor of Millbrook.

entries.title: Take their ground
entries.summary: A force that holds a place — a toll gang's chain-post, a crown's feast hall, a guild's counting-house — can now be assaulted by your band, and a breakthrough makes the place yours.
entries.detail: Your band could already clash, but always against a number with nobody behind it. Now, where somebody holds ground you are standing on, the GM can name their place and the fight is against that garrison at that power's own quality. What it costs them stays cost: a post ground down over three attempts is weaker on the fourth. A breakthrough takes the place and it becomes one of your holdings, taken from them; anything less and they held it — which is a real outcome, not a beat to smooth over. Losing every place they hold does not finish them, because a force with people left can come back for it. And it is yours in your world only: the same place is still theirs in everybody else's.

entries.title: A second Maren gets a surname
entries.summary: The world no longer hands out a name somebody already has. When the GM writes a name that belongs to someone you have met, the new person gets a family name instead — and a name nobody else has is left exactly as written.
entries.detail: The check that stops a name being reused compared whole names, so "Sera Vail" and "Sera the Scaffold" looked like two different names instead of one name twice. Now every unused given name in a tradition is spent before any is repeated, and a repeat has to carry a family name never paired with it — so fourteen people are fourteen distinct names. If the GM writes a bare name that is already somebody else’s, the new person is given a family name, which also works when the person you already know wears a title. A one-word name nobody else has is left alone: the fiction may mean it.

entries.title: Two people called Maren are two people
entries.summary: The guard that stops the world reusing a name could not see anyone with a title — so Elder Senna counted as a person whose name was "elder", and the real Senna, Coll and Ilma were invisible to it.
entries.detail: Four characters on this device have met a Maren. The check that keeps the world from handing out the same name twice read only the first word of a name, so every person holding an office was counted under their office instead: "elder" was being tallied as the given name of three separate people while Senna, Coll, Ilma, Vreni and Dresh were invisible. It reads past the office now. The GM is also asked for a whole name rather than a single one — given and family at least, a middle name where the fiction allows — and for a title when somebody holds one, which is shown beside their name in your people list with the whole name on hover.

entries.title: Raiders can have a name, and who holds a road can change how dangerous it is
entries.summary: The engine can now read a power that holds ground — a toll gang, a barony, a council — so a raid on your hold is drawn from that power's own people, their losses stick, and clearing them makes the road safer. No such power is in the world yet; this is the half that reads them.
entries.detail: Until now a raid on one of your holdings was resolved against a number: as many anonymous raiders as the place was dangerous. The band and legion machinery has been sitting there since it was built with nobody on the other side of the field. Now, where a power holds or reaches a place, the raid comes from that power's own strength, is named in the line you read, and the people it loses are gone for good — so grinding a band down is worth doing rather than something you re-roll next week. And who is standing on a place moves its danger up or down: a toll gang makes a road worse, a smugglers' arrangement can make a coast quieter, and breaking them puts it back. Nothing has changed anywhere no power stands, which today is everywhere — the content that fills this in is still being written.

entries.title: The Ent Grove is at the Crossing
entries.summary: The grove where Silas named himself to the Ent now stands inside the Crossing, a short walk from the Hundred Markets and the Great Coliseum — where his own story put it.
entries.detail: The grove was made the moment the story walked into it, before anything had decided where it was, and then two separate passes each answered that question for themselves and both got it wrong: one filed it deep in the Deepwood on the other side of the world, the other out in the valley beside the Pale March Waygate — which was simply the only road the new place happened to have. It sits where the chronicle always said it did: north through the Hub's quieter lanes, the city's buildings visible between the trees, a short walk on from the Coliseum. It keeps its own name and everything anyone remembers about it; the record now carries the ring of old trees, the low stone, the healed carvings, the two figures in the branches, and the standing fact that the Ent receives intention rather than craft. If your own save had it out in the valley, that is corrected the next time you load, and you will be told.

entries.title: A character that would not open
entries.summary: A save whose world record was missing a field crashed on load — a blank screen and nothing else. It opens now, and the days it was owed are still paid.
entries.detail: The world tick read one field of the world record without checking it was there. That field was added to the game after some saves were written, so those saves threw as the character opened — and because the tick runs while the play screen is being built, the throw took the whole screen with it. Nothing was damaged; the character simply could not be opened. The tick now fills in anything missing before it starts, which also covers four sibling fields with the same exposure. A save parked on day 3 and opened on day 40 still advances all thirty-seven days rather than starting its clock today.

entries.title: See the power field, and turn its sources on and off
entries.summary: The region map now draws the power field as real ground rather than a wash between dots, shows the authored wells and sinks, and lets you switch each source off to see what the world looks like without it.
entries.detail: The field is evaluated everywhere, not interpolated between places — the old region map coloured each place by its strength and washed between them, and said so in its own caption. Six sources can be switched on and off and the picture re-renders; each shows what share of the region it holds. The forty-four authored wells and sinks are drawn for the first time, to scale, with their names and their draw — blue for a well, red for a sink — and they can be hidden along with the waygates. The ground keeps its full brightness and all its relief: the field is blended so it lends its colour without dimming anything, and the source names are dark ink with a light halo so they read over bright uplands and dark water alike. Inside a place, a side list gives the ambient reading where you stand, the nearest anchor, and every well or sink you own or carry, with what each contributes.

entries.title: The Crossing's places are in the Crossing
entries.summary: The Axis Gate, the Great Coliseum, the Hundred Markets and the Quiet House are now inside the city they belong to — a short walk apart instead of a fortnight.
entries.detail: All four said they were part of the Crossing and the map drew them inside it, but each one actually stood eleven to eighteen days' walk away. They sit inside it now: the gate at the hub's heart, the markets on the road out to the Coliseum, and the Quiet House a long walk to the edge of the city, which is what its own description always said. Walking across the Crossing takes under a day. The ground's power reading rose very slightly everywhere in the city, because the hub's gate now sits at the hub's centre. One side-effect worth knowing: the walk from Millbrook to the Crossing is about thirteen days shorter, because the road passes through the Axis Gate on the way in.

entries.title: A stairway down is a stairway, not a week's journey
entries.summary: Somewhere reached by going below ground can now be part of the place above it. The Regulator Chamber is a short descent under the Null Stone rather than 4.8 days away.
entries.detail: Going down one level cost 4.8 walking days no matter what was down there, so a chamber at the bottom of a stair was as far off as another town and the game had to call it a separate settlement. Now, when two places sit at the same spot and one is below the other, the distance between them is the descent itself — about four hours a level. Journeys between genuinely separate underground layers are unchanged: the Unlit Deep, Archive Hollow, the Leaden Deep and the Service Ways are all exactly as far as they were. Four pairs of places in the whole world moved, and every one of them was the chamber beneath the Crossing's hub.

entries.title: Appoint a keeper from the card that says you have none
entries.summary: The holdings card now lets you make someone keeper, shows what an unkept hold really earns, and stops suggesting things about other characters' places.
entries.detail: A holding card could tell you it was unkept and that it would not climb, and give you no way to appoint anybody — the control was hidden behind Manage this place. It is on the card now, using the same list of people the other buttons use. The income line was also still reading as though an unkept hold sells nothing, and it under-counted what was already in the store. And a suggestion about a holding belonging to another of your characters no longer appears on this one.

entries.title: A hold with people in it earns
entries.summary: A holding without a keeper still sells what it makes — and a keeper can no longer be lost without anyone saying so.
entries.detail: A thriving place with a hand and a guard standing on it was producing goods and selling none of them, because only a keeper could sell — so it filled its shed, fell into arrears, and showed no income. The hands sell now, at half what a keeper would, so a keeper is still worth appointing and a place with people in it is no longer a place that earns nothing. A hold with nobody on it still earns nothing. And a keeper can no longer vanish from the record in silence: your holding's own history is read on load and gives back the keeper it still names.

entries.title: A woman is recorded as a woman
entries.summary: Sex and gender now agree on every person, and a gender already on the record fills in the sex.
entries.detail: The two were kept as separate answers and could disagree — so somebody could be written as a woman and recorded with the wrong sex, which quietly decided who she could ever be close to. They agree now, and the gender is the one that leads: anyone already described gets the matching sex, which settled it for seventy-seven people at once. A being with no sex at all — a construct, a made thing — is the one case that needs no gender either.

entries.title: People you meet get a sex, and you can set it
entries.summary: The guide was leaving sex unrecorded on most people, which quietly meant they could never be romanced — and nothing said so.
entries.detail: Sex was recorded for about one person in eight, while gender was recorded for five in six, because the rule the guide reads named one and not the other. An unrecorded sex means a person can never be romanced, and nothing anywhere told you that was why. The guide is now told to set it for everyone — with “none” as a real answer for a being that has no sex — and Repair character now lists who is missing one and lets you say it yourself.

entries.title: When the cloud list is empty, it says why
entries.summary: An empty list of cloud characters now tells you whether the world is empty or the app simply cannot see it — and Settings can test the connection.
entries.detail: If the repository details or access token were wrong, the app said “no players found” — the same thing it says when the shared world really is empty — because a private repository answers “not found” to a token that cannot read it. It now tells the two apart and says which one it is, and Settings has a Test the connection button that checks what you have typed before you save it.

entries.title: A choice that could not be taken
entries.summary: Picking an option that mentioned a place by a common name could raise a journey you never asked for, and leave you unable to go on.
entries.detail: Choosing to walk down to the wayhouse could be read as setting out for a place of that name five months away — and the question it raised could not be answered: declining threw the action away, and taking it again asked the same question. A guess at where you mean to go now stays in the region you are standing in, saying no to a journey lets you get on with what you were actually doing, and any such question already waiting on a save is cleared when it loads.

entries.title: The people you know reach the world
entries.summary: Someone you have met three times, or who set you on a quest, becomes somebody the whole world knows exists.
entries.detail: Until now the shared world knew about legends and almost nobody else. The wayhouse sister you had spoken with seventeen times existed only in your own record, so another traveler's guide had no way of knowing she was already there. Now anyone you have met three times, or who gave you a quest, is published as a person of the world — who they are, where you first saw them, and that it was you who met them. What you privately know about them stays yours.

entries.title: Everyone you meet has a name
entries.summary: People you meet are real people with names, even before you learn what they are called.
entries.detail: The hostel-keeper, the messenger, the grey-braided woman at the common house — the game was filing them under what they do, because nothing ever gave them a name. Now everyone has one from the moment you meet them. You still call them what you would call a stranger until the moment you learn better, and your guide knows who they really are in the meantime, so they stay the same person from one week to the next. Eighteen people you have already met have been given theirs.

entries.title: The world remembers who, not just what
entries.summary: What happens in one person's game now reaches another's with the people in it named.
entries.detail: The shared record of what travelers have done was reaching other players' guides with the people stripped out of it — "a wayhouse healer" where it could have said Sister Vreni, whom the game already knew by name, role and seventeen meetings. So the next guide to read it invented a second Vreni. A record of something that happened now carries the people it happened to, and anything written before is still read exactly as it was.

entries.title: A quest can be lost
entries.summary: Quests can now ask you to decide something mid-way, and they can end badly — including by running out of time.
entries.detail: Until now a quest asked you for exactly one choice, at the very end, and every ending was a different kind of success. A stage can now put a real decision in front of you — which of three things to give a dying man, say — where each has its own cost and shuts some doors behind it. And a quest can now be lost: an ending can be a failure, with consequences as durable as any other, and a quest with a deadline can simply run out of days while you are elsewhere. You will see the days remaining, and you will be warned before they are gone.

entries.title: Quests stop telling you the answer
entries.summary: A quest can now keep a secret from you, and a correction to a quest reaches the one you are already playing.
entries.detail: A quest had nowhere to keep anything back: every field an author could write was a field somebody said out loud, so a quest about working out what is wrong with a patient told you what was wrong with him. Quests now have a place for the things you are meant to work out yourself — the guide knows them, and will let you earn them rather than hand them over. And a fix to a quest now reaches a quest you have already started, including an ending that was added after you began; before, a new ending would appear as a button that refused to do anything.

entries.title: The power field knows what it is standing on
entries.summary: The field engine reads the world's forty-four authored power sources by name, and can be sampled at any scale.
entries.detail: The extracted field engine was reading a baked list of forty-three anonymous sources, so it could tell you how strong the ground was and not what it belonged to. It now reads the authored records: the Axis Gate is the Axis Gate, a crystal well, and whether the nanite around it is ordered, wild or cleared comes from the region it sits in. The same evaluator can now be asked for any window of the world at any resolution, which is what the world, region and location maps will each draw from — one field instead of three that disagree.

entries.title: The power field has an engine of its own
entries.summary: The way the world's powers are shown and applied - evaluated everywhere rather than drawn as pins - is now part of the game instead of a prototype page.
entries.detail: Nothing changes in play yet. The field is evaluated for every point of the world: the substrate density, what the nanite is doing, where the veil is thin, and how much meaning a place carries - with wells that raise the ground and sinks that draw it down, and with the arcs of the story shifting the whole field as they move. The tables it needs, which existed only inside a prototype page, are now part of the world's own files.

entries.title: Pictures come back
entries.summary: The game draws pictures again, through a service of our own — and the pictures you already have keep the faces you know.
entries.detail: The service the game used began charging for new pictures on 19 September, which is why drawing stopped. Pictures now come from our own service instead. It keeps every picture it serves, so a picture is drawn once and then it is yours; and when it meets a picture it has not seen, it asks the old service first and keeps THAT picture, so the faces and places you already know do not change. Only what the old service can no longer give us is drawn anew. Your saves are updated the first time you open them, and nothing you already have is lost.

entries.title: Send a band on a mission
entries.summary: A band can go on one of the seven errands (trade, escort, carry word, watch, seek, work a place, treat with) and work at it as a team — whoever of them is free to leave.
entries.detail: On the Bands tab, Send on a mission… says who would go and who would stay before you send anyone: whoever walks at your side stays with you, whoever keeps or guards a hold keeps their post, and whoever is out on a job, at standing work or carrying a charge of their own goes on with it. What the band can be sent to do is judged on the ones who go. Whoever of them is best at each part of the work rolls it, every three days, like any charge on the Jobs tab. Those who went cannot be called, sent on a job or brought to your side until they are back, and the GM is told where they went and who with. A mission that goes wrong costs them heads and they stay out; you can recall them at any time, and the charge ends there.

entries.title: Raise a hold's features to level 2 and 3
entries.summary: Walls, shrines, quarters, mines, forges and smithies can be raised a level, as a job, and each level makes them do more.
entries.detail: On a hold's card, ⇧ beside a feature shows what raising it would do (more defence, more aura and pilgrims, room for more hands, a bigger yield, or more made at a forge), what it costs from the hold's store, the work it takes, and the upkeep after. Make it a job and it goes on the Jobs board with its materials set aside. A success raises it; if the work falls short, the materials go back to the store.

entries.title: Standing work at your holds
entries.summary: Put people and hands with no job to work at a hold: foraging, hunting, training, mending, guarding, patrolling, tending, or keeping the accounts.
entries.detail: Each hold's card has a Standing work section. Put someone to a kind of work and see their chance of a good day. Every good day banks toward something that lasts: raw material, living stock, better-trained hands, a hold in better condition. Some work changes the hold while it is done: guards and patrols stand the watch against raids, tending lifts the yields, and kept accounts lower the upkeep. Everyone at work is paid a hand's wage each pass, and while they work they cannot be sent on jobs or counted in a band's turn.

entries.title: Companions at their own level
entries.summary: A companion who is a figure of the world in their own right now shows their own level, not yours.
entries.detail: Companions were shown at your level, as a floor, even when they are much more than that. Maren, a legendary warden, read as level 33 beside Silas when she stands in her sixties. A companion now stands at the higher of your level and their own, everywhere their level is shown or used.

entries.title: The Party tab
entries.summary: Set how each ally at your side fights: their stance, the crafts they prefer, and who is brought forward.
entries.detail: Each ally can be cautious, balanced or aggressive, which decides what they reach for in a fight, and you can star the crafts they should prefer, like your own boosts. Choose who is brought forward to be told by name, within how many you can lead. Roll a round to see exactly what the storyteller will be handed. In a fight, every turn now rolls each ally's chosen craft and tells what happened, instead of leaving it to invention.

entries.title: A band's turn by stance, and the Legion tab
entries.summary: Give each band a stance and see who does what on its turn; the new Legion tab adds its bands up.
entries.detail: On the Bands tab, each band shows one turn at the stance you choose: how many read the ground, guard, mend, strike, move or break, who takes each part (everyone doing what they are best at next to the rest), and how many are expected to land. The Legion tab shows a legion's turn as its bands' turns added together, each by its own stance, and lets you choose who commands it.

entries.title: Three allies all act, and nobody sits twice
entries.summary: With three allies at your side, all three now act in a fight, as the rule says; and a companion who is also in your company counts once.
entries.detail: The fight was counting you among your allies, so a party of three read as four and one of them was left to the line. And a companion who had also joined your company was seated twice, so an enemy could pick them twice. Both are fixed: three allies all take a real turn, and every person has one seat.

entries.title: Honest word when pictures can't be drawn
entries.summary: New pictures can't be drawn right now, and the game now says why instead of asking you to try again.
entries.detail: The service that draws the game's pictures has begun to charge for each new one, so none can be drawn at the moment. When a picture fails for that reason, the viewer and the gallery now say so plainly instead of offering another try that would fail the same way. Every picture you already have is safe and still shows.

entries.title: An armory at your holds
entries.summary: A forge or smithy at your hold makes swords, axes, bows, crossbows, shields and armour, and your troops can be outfitted from it.
entries.detail: On a hold with a forge or smithy, order what it should make and how many; each pass it works the order from the store's raw material, and says so if the material runs out. Standing in the hold, open the Bands tab and choose Outfit on a body of hands: one weapon, one shield and one piece of armour each, up to what the armory holds. Each piece makes them better in a fight, and shields on at least half of them let them protect, so they lose fewer. You can also sell gear from the armory, at the place's price for arms.

entries.title: Your holds' news reaches you again
entries.summary: What your holds did while you were away (sales, upkeep, raids, work finished) is told to you again.
entries.detail: When you came back without your character's day having moved, your holds still worked (they sold, paid their keep, and finished what they were given) but the news of it was lost on the way to you. It now reaches the flash, the News tab and the story. Passes that already happened are not told again; everything from the next one on is.

entries.title: A vault at your holds
entries.summary: Keep valuables at a hold you own: statues, artifacts, and wells and sinks that work on the ground there.
entries.detail: Stand in your hold and choose Put in the vault. Whole stacks move from your pack into the hold and wait there until you come back for them; a thing the story carries stays with you. A well or sink kept in the vault works on the ground at that place, so every craft worked there feels it, and the roll's note names it. Take things back the same way, where the hold stands; a full pack says so rather than losing anything.

entries.title: Switch wells and sinks on and off
entries.summary: Every charged thing you carry or keep, and every companion's aura, can be switched off and on again.
entries.detail: A well thickens the ground and a sink thins it, which helps some crafts and hurts others. Switch one off from its card in your pack, from its place in a hold's vault, or, for a companion's aura, from their row in your company. Switched off, it moves nothing until you switch it on, and the story knows it is quiet.

entries.title: Charged things you carry now count
entries.summary: A Waystaff, or any other charged thing in your pack, now changes the ground around you as it was always meant to.
entries.detail: These things lost their charge on the way into your pack, so carrying one changed nothing. They now count, and the note on a roll names what you carry that moved the ground.

entries.title: A starting purse
entries.summary: A new character begins with money that fits their background, in the money of the place they start.
entries.detail: What you begin with is what your old life let you carry away: a trader's stock travels, a temple's wealth stays with the temple. It is never enough to decide which background to choose — at most enough for a few valuable things. Begin in a Reach and it is that Reach's scrip: more of it, and good only there until you change it.

entries.title: Money you were owed
entries.summary: Characters who were never given a starting purse have been paid one, and paid for the deeds already on their record.
entries.detail: Two payments, in the money of where you stand now: the starting purse you should have had, if you are below it, and eight shards' worth for every deed on your record — the same for every deed. The game tells you both the first time you open the character.

entries.title: Soldiers on a job are paid
entries.summary: Sending a band's soldiers or a hold's guards on a job costs their wage for the time they are away.
entries.detail: The Jobs tab shows the wages before you send anyone — so many soldiers, at a wage each, for each three days away — and adds them to the job's cost. Their food comes out of that pay, so nothing is taken from a hold's stores, which are kept for battles and journeys.

entries.title: What you buy in the story costs money
entries.summary: Buying, being paid, selling and finding money in a scene now move your purse.
entries.detail: Until now the Game Master could not see your purse and had no way to charge or pay you, so a purchase in the story cost nothing and a reward never arrived. Now it sees what you carry and the money of the place, and every payment settles in that money — or, if you cannot pay, it does not happen, and the game says so under the scene.

entries.title: Sell what you carry at your hold
entries.summary: Standing at a hold of yours, you can sell the things in your pack for the local price.
entries.detail: Open a hold's card while you stand there and choose Sell from your pack: every thing you carry is listed with what it fetches in that place's own money, and you tick what to sell. Things the story is carrying are kept, and a place that has no use for something says so. Prices differ by place — the same knife fetches more where knives are wanted.

entries.title: Change money
entries.summary: Change one kind of money for another at the Crossing, or at a hold of yours by that place's rates.
entries.detail: The Crossing changes anything for anything and takes a modest cut. A Reach changes its own scrip for the money it wants — a better rate than the Crossing when you bring that money in, a worse one when you take it out — and will not touch money it does not want. You see what you would get before anything changes hands.

entries.title: The news is kept
entries.summary: A News tab on your character holds everything the world has told you, so nothing you missed is lost.
entries.detail: Newest first, by world-day, with filters for the world, your own work, word from elsewhere, and updates. A fight in the log opens just as it does when it first arrives. When the game is updated, the news says so — with the notes one tap away — and that line is kept too.

entries.title: A long time away no longer drops news
entries.summary: News waiting for you is no longer cut to the last twenty lines before you see it.

entries.title: What's new
entries.summary: After an update, the game tells you what changed.
entries.detail: A banner after an update says how many new things and fixes arrived since you last played. Open it for the list, and open any line for the detail. The version number on the title screen and in the top bar opens these notes at any time, back through the whole 2.x line.

entries.title: Version numbers mean something now
entries.summary: The last number moves with every update, the middle one when five new features have landed, and the first only when the game becomes a different game.
entries.detail: Until now every update moved only the last number, which is how the game reached 2.0.100. From 2.1.0 the middle number marks a real step: it moves on the update that brings the fifth new feature since it last moved. The first number moves only when the game changes what it is for someone already playing.

summaries.title: What the 2.0 line brought
summaries.summary: A world you share with other travellers, journeys and jobs, holds that grow, and money that depends on where you stand.

entries.title: Other travellers share your world
entries.summary: Other players' characters are part of your world now.
entries.detail: You can meet another traveller in town, send word to them through someone you both know, and trade with their holds through their keepers. A crisis one of you answers reads as answered for everyone. The people the world makes, and what is true of them, are shared — what you know of them stays yours.

entries.title: Journeys you plan and walk
entries.summary: A journey is agreed, readied, then walked leg by leg.
entries.detail: A dangerous leg is planned before you take it, and a stopped journey can be taken up again. Your travel and gathering crafts carry the road. Where you keep mounts, you ride, and the road is shorter.

entries.title: Jobs and errands
entries.summary: Send your people — and your troops — to get things done.
entries.detail: A job has a place, a difficulty and a reward. The people you send roll their own dice for it, travel there on their own road, and come back when it is done. People in your charge work their errands by the same dice, and a band's hands or a hold's guards can be sent too.

entries.title: Holds that grow
entries.summary: A hold has room, and grows into a bigger place.
entries.detail: Building needs room. When a hold is full, thriving and has lasted a season, you are offered its next size. A training yard cuts the cost of calling troops, an infirmary heals the hurt and slows how fast the dead sink, and barracks house your soldiers — a band with no bed is quartered at a cost.

entries.title: Money depends on where you stand
entries.summary: The world's five kinds of money are in play.
entries.detail: Each place pays in its own money and takes the others at a worse rate. A hold in a Reach earns that Reach's scrip and pays its keep from it. Your purse says what money the place you stand in takes.

entries.title: Every roll says how it lands
entries.summary: Five ways a roll can land, on every skill, shown before you choose.
entries.detail: A critical success, a success, a partial, a failure or a critical failure, with the odds of each on the choice. A skill says what it rolls, a choice that uses a craft rolls that craft, and even a trained hand can fail badly.

entries.title: People who practise and fight as themselves
entries.summary: Everyone you know has crafts, and fights with them.
entries.detail: Someone you have met fights as themselves when a fight comes. The world's figures sit on seven rungs of power, so a new character meets people of their own scale.

entries.title: News that finds you
entries.summary: Near news stands out, and a strike against you is a scene.
entries.detail: What happens near you is marked as near. A strike aimed at you becomes a scene: a guard can fight beside you, and the one who came for you can be questioned. A fight in the news can be opened to see it.

entries.title: A year with seasons
entries.summary: The world keeps one year, with early, middle and late seasons.
entries.detail: The seasons belong to the world, not to your character, and they turn fewer times near the ring.

entries.title: Gates and roads
entries.summary: A made gate leads to the hub, and roads run both ways.
entries.detail: A gate you make joins the network and leads to the hub through it, and a road once found can be walked back.

entries.title: Reload when you choose
entries.summary: A newer build offers a Reload button instead of reloading under you.
entries.detail: While you play on an old build nothing it writes goes up, and the banner says so — but the reload is yours to take.

entries.title: Rolled actions work again
entries.summary: For about six hours on 18 September, every action that rolled dice failed.
entries.detail: It was fixed the same day, and every file is now checked on each update so a mistake of that kind cannot reach the game again.

entries.title: Your crafts, pushed, are yours to try
entries.summary: The game no longer refuses a craft you hold when you push it somewhere new.
entries.detail: Pushing a craft past its usual use is rolled as a push — harder, and riskier — and the Game Master decides what it does. It is never refused before the dice are thrown.

entries.title: A value that did not exist was tilting rolls
entries.summary: Most saves carried a spectrum value with no meaning, and it moved rolls by up to 15 points.
entries.detail: It came from a placeholder the Game Master copied into its choices. It is set aside, kept but no longer counted, and only the world's twelve spectrum axes can reach your character now.

entries.title: One person, one record
entries.summary: People the world had doubled are one person again, and people it had confused are two.
entries.detail: Halvex is one man again, and several people who had been mixed up with someone else are their own person.

entries.title: Test runs stay out of your save
entries.summary: The game's own checks can no longer write into a real character.

entries.title: Who is playing is chosen
entries.summary: A shared device asks who is playing instead of writing someone else's profile.

entries.title: A home is never raided
entries.summary: A place you make your home is not a hold, and raiders do not come for it.

entries.title: Asides say the whole sentence
entries.summary: A note from the game no longer cuts off mid-word.
